v.approach: Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles streamed into the browser
v.one_paragraph_summary: Google sells the same 3D "photo-mesh" you see in Google Earth through its Map Tiles API. A browser game can stream it with the free 3DTilesRendererJS library (three.js) or CesiumJS, so the whole UIC campus and the Chicago skyline appear with real textures and almost no modeling work. Seen from above (helicopter, drone, or a high third-person camera), it looks remarkably real, and for a small game it is cheap (roughly $0 to $25 a month for 50 players). At street level, where a GTA-style character walks, it breaks down. Google's own FAQ says the mesh gives "less precise modeling of the real world at the pedestrian-scale", with "parked cars or awnings melted into the mesh" and "tree canopies ... modeled as floating objects". Lighting and shadows are baked into the photos, so there is no day/night cycle or dynamic lighting. The terms are also strict. You may not cache, pre-fetch, store or export the geometry, and you may not create content (such as 3D building models) from it. The API is "for map visualizations" only. Google's logo and data credits must always be on screen. Using it "with or near a non-Google Map" is forbidden. Players must also be told that Google's terms apply. It is not GTA 6. At best it is a strong backdrop and skyline layer to combine with hand-built hero buildings and a separate collision mesh, and even that hybrid sits in a legal gray zone you should confirm with Google.

realism.what_it_looks_like: From roughly 30 m up and higher it looks like Google Earth: real Brutalist concrete facades of University Hall and the Netsch buildings, real rooftops, the real Loop skyline, correct colors. In a high orbit or drone view it is the most 'real-looking' option per hour of effort. At eye height (about 1.7 m) with a third-person character it looks like a low-poly, texture-smeared photogrammetry sculpture. Facades are flat-projected photos, ground textures are blurry, and lighting and shadows from capture time are baked in. Google's FAQ (https://mapsplatform.google.com/resources/blog/commonly-asked-questions-about-our-recently-launched-photorealistic-3d-tiles/) says the mesh is 'generated procedurally using photogrammetric methods with flat imagery... this results in less precise modeling of the real world at the pedestrian-scale', e.g. 'parked cars or awnings melted into the mesh, or sometimes tree canopies get modeled as floating objects'. Google Earth Studio's own guidance says to 'avoid animating the camera extremely close to the ground or in between buildings, as these angles tend to reveal imperfections' (https://earth.google.com/studio/docs/best-practices/). A developer on Hacker News testing it in Unreal called ground level 'pretty weird and blobby down there' and 'a lot of the street data is pretty warped' (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=36000631).
realism.weaknesses_up_close: Melted cars, awnings, benches, light poles and bike racks fused into the ground. Trees become blobs or floating canopies. Wavy or warped walls and street surfaces. No real windows, doors or depth, only a photo on a lumpy surface. Lighting and shadows are baked in, so no dynamic sun, no night, no rain or wet-road reflections, and no PBR materials (nothing like GTA 6). Visible seams and LOD popping between tiles. Interiors are absent. Content changes when Google updates imagery and older versions cannot be locked (Cesium forum: https://community.cesium.com/t/google-photorealistic-3d-tiles-changed-over-time-is-there-any-way-to-lock-or-preserve-previous-data/44682). Google says the tiles are not 'survey-grade'. No Chicago- or UIC-specific street-level review was found; Chicago coverage is likely but not checked against Google's coverage map (unverified).

platform.runs_in_web_browser: Yes. The tiles are OGC 3D Tiles (glTF) streamed over HTTPS and rendered with 3DTilesRendererJS (three.js, npm 3d-tiles-renderer 0.5.3) or CesiumJS (npm cesium 1.146.0). This fits the existing three.js + Rapier + Colyseus plan with no platform change. Cesium for Unreal and Unity also support the tiles if the platform is ever reconsidered (https://cesium.com/learn/unreal/unreal-photorealistic-3d-tiles/).
platform.desktop: Works in desktop Chrome, Edge and Firefox with WebGL2. Moderate GPU load. Streaming bandwidth at street level is significant (tens of MB per session; exact figure unverified).
platform.phones: Possible but heavy: streaming plus memory pressure on mobile browsers. Expect lower LOD and blurrier ground on phones (unverified, no benchmark found).
platform.player_hardware_needed: Any laptop or desktop with a WebGL2-capable GPU and a decent internet connection. No gaming PC is required to view the tiles themselves.
platform.developer_hardware_needed: Agents in the GPU-less container can write and build the code and reach tile.googleapis.com (tested: the endpoint answers and returns 403 'unregistered callers' without a key, so an API key is required). Visual testing needs headless Chromium with software WebGL (SwiftShader), which is slow but works for screenshots (unverified in this container). Every test page load uses a billable root-tile request. The owner does not need a gaming PC; a normal laptop browser is enough to playtest.

v.multiplayer_fit: Good for client-side visuals: each player's browser streams its own tiles, and the Colyseus server never touches Google content. Problem: an authoritative server cannot use the Google mesh for physics, because downloading or storing tiles server-side conflicts with 'No Scraping' and 'No Caching' (ToS 3.2.3(a),(b)). Server physics therefore needs a separate collision world, e.g. from Overture/OSM footprints plus a flat ground or terrain plane, and that world will not match the lumpy Google ground exactly. Client-side, raycasting against loaded tiles to plant feet works technically (Cesium does 'clamp to ground' on these tiles). However, Google's FAQ says 'reading and recording measurements (heights, distances, elevations, etc.) from our 3D imagery is considered derivative and is prohibited', so even runtime ground-sampling is a gray area (unverified how Google interprets this for games). Each player needs their own root-tile session (billing below).

legal_and_licensing.finding: Google Maps Platform Terms of Service page fetched 2026-10-10 shows 'Last modified August 26, 2026'. Maps Service Specific Terms: 'Last modified June 10, 2026'. AUP: 'Last modified June 23, 2026'. Material changes take effect 30 days after notice (section 1.2(b)).

Nothing in the ToS prohibits games. The license is to use the Services in a 'Customer Application', defined as 'any web page or application ... that has material value independent of the Services' (sections 3.1 and 20). A game with missions has independent value. 3.2.3(d) bars products 'substantially similar to' Google products, which a mission game is not. Google also ran an entertainment prize category for 3D Tiles experiences. No explicit Google statement saying 'games are allowed' was found.

As reported by search snippets of the policy page (the page itself is blocked from this container): 'Applications should use Map Tiles API for map visualizations. You may not use Map Tiles API for any non-visualization use cases' such as image analysis, machine interpretation, object detection or identification, geodata extraction or resale, and offline uses. The Google FAQ adds that 'reading and recording measurements (heights, distances, elevations, etc.) from our 3D imagery is considered derivative and is prohibited.' This makes using tile geometry for physics or collision a gray area.

ToS 3.2.3(a) No Scraping, verbatim: 'Customer will not export, extract, or otherwise scrape Google Maps Content for use outside the Services. For example, Customer will not: (i) pre-fetch, index, store, reshare, or rehost Google Maps Content outside the services; (ii) bulk download Google Maps tiles...'. 3.2.3(b), verbatim: 'Customer will not cache Google Maps Content except as expressly permitted under the Maps Service Specific Terms.' The Service Specific Terms (June 10, 2026) contain no Map Tiles API caching permission (checked by text search). So there is no offline mode, no packaging tiles into the game build, no service-worker tile cache, and no exporting the mesh to Blender or a collision file.

legal_and_licensing.topic: Creating content / modeling buildings from the tiles
legal_and_licensing.finding: ToS 3.2.3(c), verbatim: 'Customer will not create content based on Google Maps Content. For example, Customer will not: (i) trace or digitize roadways, building outlines... (ii) create 3D building models from 45° Imagery...'. Hero buildings must not be modeled or traced from Google 3D tiles or imagery. They should be built from the owner's own photos, Overture/OSM footprints, or other licensed sources.

ToS 3.2.1(a) bars 'copy, modify, create a derivative work of, reverse engineer...' (in context, aimed at the Services and source code). Attribution must not be modified (3.2.2(b)). There is no explicit clause on hiding or clipping parts of the 3D mesh. Cesium, a Google partner, publishes an official tutorial clipping Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles to inset a custom model (https://cesium.com/learn/cesiumjs-learn/cesiumjs-clipping-polygons/). A Cesium forum answer says clipping third-party data server-side in Cesium ion is not allowed. Google's formal position on client-side clipping or replacement is unverified.

ToS 3.2.3(e), verbatim: 'To avoid quality issues and/or brand confusion, Customer will not use the Google Maps Core Services with or near a non-Google Map in a Customer Application. For example, Customer will not ... (iii) link a Google Map to non-Google Maps Content or a non-Google Map.' Showing an OSM/Overture-based minimap, or rendering OSM-derived buildings next to Google tiles, risks violating this. Whether an invisible collision mesh from Overture/OSM counts as a 'non-Google Map' is unclear (unverified). The policies also have a 'hybrid visualizations' section requiring the audience to clearly understand which data is Google's; its full text could not be read.

ToS 3.2.2(b): 'Customer will display all attribution that (i) Google provides through the Services (including branding, logos, and copyright and trademark notices)... Customer will not modify, obscure, or delete such attribution.' The Map Tiles policies (via search snippets) require the Google Maps logo visible and unaltered, and full data attribution strings that change with the viewport, gathered from each tile's glTF asset.copyright, sorted and displayed, usually bottom-right. Other logos must not overlap them and need a buffer. This applies to promotional videos too. The game HUD must permanently reserve a corner for this.

Allowed and intended. Google's launch blog says the tiles let you 'use the renderer of your choice and overlay your own data'. Cesium and Google co-promote overlays such as BIM models. No clause forbids drawing characters on top.

legal_and_licensing.topic: Game's own Terms of Service flow-down
legal_and_licensing.finding: ToS 3.2.2(a)(i): the game's terms must notify users that it 'includes Google Maps features and content' and that use is subject to the Google Maps/Google Earth Additional Terms of Service (https://maps.google.com/help/terms_maps/) and the Google Privacy Policy. The owner must publish a ToS page for the game.

ToS 3.2.1(c)(vi): the Services may not be used 'in a Customer Application that would be deemed to be a "Website or online service directed to children" under the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA).' A campus game for university students is not directed to children, but it must not be marketed to under-13s.

ToS 3.2.1(c)(ii)(1) bars use 'in a manner intended to ... avoid incurring Fees'. Sharing one session token across players, or proxying tiles to dodge root-tile billing, would breach this. Reusing a player's own session token across page reloads within its 3-hour window is suggested by Luciad's docs; Google's view is unverified.

legal_and_licensing.topic: Cesium ion Community license and Cesium OSM Buildings
legal_and_licensing.finding: The Cesium ion Community tier is free for 'personal, non-commercial use' with a quota of 1,000 Google Photorealistic root tiles per month (Commercial: 5,000, Premium: 10,000), per the pricing page as reported by search. Cesium OSM Buildings is OSM data under ODbL and requires '© OpenStreetMap contributors' attribution. It is a plain grey or white extruded-box layer, not photorealistic. Mixing it with Google tiles also hits the 'non-Google map' clause.

ai_agent_buildability.explanation: Technically easy. The 3DTilesRendererJS GoogleCloudAuthPlugin handles keys, session tokens and attribution collection, and TilesAttributionOverlay shows credits. An ECEF-to-local transform puts UIC at the origin, and agents can wire a three.js scene in a day or two. Hard parts: (1) placing a walking character on lumpy, streamed, sometimes-missing geometry without exporting it; (2) aligning a separate Overture/OSM collision world with the Google mesh; (3) visual QA from a GPU-less container (software WebGL screenshots are slow, and every test burns a billable root request); (4) the legal gray areas, which agents cannot resolve.

v.owner_effort: Create a Google Cloud account and a billing account with a credit card. Enable the Map Tiles API and create an API key. Restrict the key: application restriction = HTTP referrers (websites) set to the game's domain(s) and localhost for testing; API restriction = Map Tiles API only. Google 'strongly recommends' restricting keys (https://developers.google.cn/maps/documentation/tile/get-api-key?hl=en). Set a daily quota cap (e.g. 200 root requests per day) and a budget alert, because the key is visible to anyone who opens the browser dev tools and referrer headers can be spoofed outside browsers. Optionally try the no-card 'Maps Demo Key' for prototyping; whether it covers Map Tiles API is unverified (https://mapsplatform.google.com/maps-demo-key/). Publish a game Terms of Service page with the Google flow-down text. Ideally email Google Maps Platform sales or support to confirm in writing that (a) a third-person game, (b) client-side ground raycasting, (c) clipping out a few buildings and replacing them with custom models, and (d) a hidden collision mesh from Overture/OSM data are acceptable. Playtest in a normal browser.
risks: Fails the owner's main goal: street-level realism is nowhere near GTA 6 (melted cars, blobby trees, warped walls, baked lighting, no night or weather). Google's own FAQ says so.

Physics and collision gray area: the policies say 'visualization only' and the FAQ says reading heights or distances from the 3D imagery is 'derivative and is prohibited'. Using the mesh for collision or raycasting could be judged non-compliant.
The 'No Use With Non-Google Maps' clause (3.2.3(e)) may conflict with mixing in OSM/Overture-derived geometry or an OSM minimap.
No caching or offline use: the game cannot ship the map, every player depends on Google live, and an outage or key suspension blanks the world.
Content drift: Google updates the mesh and older versions cannot be locked, so hand-placed hero buildings, mission markers and collision may stop lining up.
The API key is public in the browser. Abuse is mitigated by referrer restriction plus quota caps, but spoofed referrers are possible outside browsers.
Mandatory Google logo and attribution permanently on the HUD, and in trailers and videos.
Google can request app review (3.2.2(c)) and suspend for AUP violations after 24 hours' notice. Terms can change on 30 days' notice.
Cesium ion Community is non-commercial only, and Cesium forum posts say clipping third-party (Google) data in ion is not allowed.

Several policy-page quotes in this report come from search snippets because developers.google.com and mapsplatform.google.com are blocked from this container. The owner can unblock developers.google.com, mapsplatform.google.com and cesium.com so they can be verified.
v.can_combine_with: Best used as a distant and aerial layer in a hybrid. (1) Hand-modeled or photogrammetry 'hero' buildings for the walkable core (University Hall, Student Center East, Daley Library, the Quad), built from the owner's own photos, never from Google content, placed by clipping out the Google mesh in those spots (Cesium clipping-polygon technique; Google's position unverified). (2) A separate invisible collision and physics world built from Overture/OSM footprints and heights plus a ground plane, used by both Rapier on clients and the Colyseus server (legally safer than raycasting Google geometry, but may brush against the 'non-Google map' clause). (3) A procedural or Overture-extruded city fallback that works offline and with no key. A cleaner split: use Google tiles only for a 'fly-over / campus tour' mode or skyline backdrop beyond a radius of about 300 m, and keep the walkable game world fully owned. Not combinable with a shipped or offline build, server-side use of the geometry, or exporting the mesh into Blender or Unreal assets.
v.verdict_for_this_project: Do not use Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles as the main walkable world. It cannot meet the 'GTA 6-like, buildings look real up close' bar: Google itself says the mesh is imprecise at pedestrian scale, and lighting is baked so dynamic GTA-style lighting is impossible. The terms also block the things a game world needs: caching, exporting geometry for collision, building models from it, and probably mixing it with OSM-based maps. It is cheap (about $3 to $25 a month for 50 players), quick to integrate in three.js, and excellent from the air. Recommended role: an optional 'Google Earth-style' backdrop and skyline layer, or a fly-over intro, with custom-built hero buildings and an owned collision world doing the real work. Get Google's written OK before relying on the hybrid. If realism at street level is the top priority, the owned-asset path (custom PBR models with photo-based textures, possibly in Unreal/Unity rather than the browser) is the one that can approach the goal.

key_claims_to_verify.claim: ToS 3.2.3(a)-(c),(e) (Aug 26, 2026 version) prohibit pre-fetching, storing, caching, exporting, creating 3D models from Google Maps Content, and use 'with or near a non-Google Map'. Quoted verbatim from the fetched page.

Map Tiles policies say 'You may not use Map Tiles API for any non-visualization use cases' (search snippet only; page blocked here). This is critical for whether collision or raycasting on tiles is allowed.

Google FAQ: the mesh is 'less precise ... at the pedestrian-scale', with 'parked cars or awnings melted into the mesh', and 'reading and recording measurements (heights, distances, elevations, etc.) ... is considered derivative and is prohibited'.
Photorealistic 3D Tiles is an Enterprise SKU: 1,000 free root requests per month, then $6.00 per 1,000 down to $2.40 at 5M+ (search snippet of the pricing list).
One root tileset request gives at least 3 hours of tile requests. Tile requests are not billed. Quota is 10,000 root requests per day.
Cesium ion Community: free, non-commercial, 1,000 Google root tiles per month. Commercial $149/month for 5,000.
Clipping or hiding parts of Google tiles client-side to insert custom hero buildings is acceptable to Google (only Cesium's tutorial supports this; no Google statement found).

v.approach: Web-native realistic meshes (three.js WebGPU + PBR + accurate data)
v.one_paragraph_summary: Under this approach, the UIC East Campus is built as real 3D models that run in an ordinary web browser using three.js, a free graphics library. Building outlines come from Overture/OpenStreetMap. Heights and roof shapes come from free government laser scans (LiDAR): Cook County's 2017 USGS scan (93.7 billion points) is downloadable from this container right now. Surfaces use free, public-domain photo-scanned materials such as concrete, brick, asphalt and grass, plus a real photographed sky, real-time shadows and modern lighting effects. Key landmarks such as University Hall get hand-tuned or procedurally generated facades, ideally textured from photos the owner takes on campus. The honest bottom line is that this cannot reach GTA 6 quality. A well-executed browser campus in 2026 can look like a good mid-2010s console or PC game, roughly GTA V on PS4, in aerial and wide views, and somewhat weaker at street level. It will not match GTA 6's dense crowds, foliage, wet-street reflections, hand-made detail or ray-traced lighting. Brutalist concrete happens to be one of the more forgiving styles to make look convincing: big simple shapes and rough grey materials. That makes UIC a better-than-average candidate for browser realism.

realism.what_it_looks_like:
Best realistic case on a decent laptop: sunlit concrete buildings with correct proportions and heights, photo-based PBR concrete and brick, soft sun shadows from cascaded shadow maps, ambient occlusion in corners, sky lighting from an HDRI or physical sky, bloom and filmic tone mapping, temporal anti-aliasing, instanced trees and street furniture. It reads like a polished architectural visualization or a 2013-2016-era open-world game (GTA V on PS4 / Watch Dogs-class lighting, at lower asset density). Aerial and mid-distance views are the strongest, because massing, shadows and materials carry the look and accurate LiDAR heights make the skyline unmistakably UIC. Brutalist precast/board-formed concrete with repetitive window grids (University Hall) suits procedural modeling plus tileable CC0 concrete materials.

The three.js r186 package (verified by downloading three@0.186.1 from npm) ships these as built-in TSL post-processing and lighting nodes: SSGI, VXGI (voxel cone-traced GI), GTAO, SSAO, SSR with a REBLUR-style recurrent denoiser, screen-space contact shadows (SSS), TRAA and TAAU (temporal upscaling), FSR1, bloom, god rays, depth of field, motion blur, CSM shadows, LightProbeGrid (baked L2 SH irradiance probes), clustered lights, SkyMesh, Water, and a native GaussianSplat object. There is also an official 'webgpu_generator_city' procedural city example (CityGenerator + LightProbeGrid + SkyMesh + 4096 shadow map). The feature set is real and current; the gap to AAA is mostly content (art hours, asset density) and GPU budget, not missing renderer features.
realism.weaknesses_up_close: 1) Facade detail at 1-3 m: tileable textures repeat. Without bespoke grime, staining, decals, mullions, real window depth and interior-mapped rooms, walls look 'CG clean'. Hand-made AAA facades have thousands of unique details per block. 2) People and NPCs: realistic animated humans are the biggest giveaway, and AI-generated or rigged characters in the browser are far from GTA 6 (MetaHuman-class) quality. 3) Vegetation: dense, wind-animated, alpha-tested trees and grass are expensive on integrated GPUs, so sparse trees look 'gamey'. 4) Global illumination: SSGI is screen-space only (artifacts at screen edges, flicker without temporal filtering), and VXGI requires static geometry and is costly. On integrated GPUs you fall back to baked probes/AO, so bounce light is approximate. GTA 6 uses ray-traced GI and reflections on consoles (unverified). 5) Reflections: wet asphalt and glass need SSR, which is costly and screen-space. 6) Texture resolution and memory: a whole campus at close-up texel density will not fit a browser download or an iGPU memory budget, so street-level surfaces will be softer than in a 100+ GB console game. 7) Interiors: there will be none, or fake parallax interiors. 8) LOD pop-in and shader compile hitches on first load (WebGPU pipeline compilation). 9) Night lighting with many lights: clustered lights exist, but each extra effect costs frames on an iGPU.

platform.runs_in_web_browser: yes. three.js r186 WebGPURenderer runs on WebGPU and falls back to a WebGL2 backend. WebGPU now ships in Chrome/Edge (113+), Firefox (141+ Windows, macOS on Apple Silicon later, Linux still in progress) and Safari 26 (macOS/iOS/iPadOS) per https://web.dev/blog/webgpu-supported-major-browsers. Some heavy effects (VXGI, compute-based denoisers) need the WebGPU path, and WebGL2-fallback players get a reduced preset. Note: three.js forum users have reported the WebGPU renderer running slower than WebGL in some scenes (https://discourse.threejs.org/t/webgpu-significant-performance-drop-and-shadow-quality-regression-in-r182-vs-webgl-r170/89322), so per-device benchmarking is required.
platform.desktop: Same build runs in any desktop browser. It can optionally be wrapped as a desktop app (Electron/Tauri), which gains nothing in graphics. A dedicated GPU desktop gets the 'Ultra' preset (SSGI/VXGI, SSR, 4K shadows).
platform.phones: Partially. WebGPU exists on Android Chrome 121+ (Android 12+, Qualcomm/ARM GPUs) and iOS/iPadOS 26 Safari (https://web.dev/blog/webgpu-supported-major-browsers), but a realistic campus would need a 'Low' preset (no SSGI/SSR, baked AO only, reduced textures, render scale ~0.5) and probably 20-30 fps (estimate, unverified). Phones would not look realistic. Treat phones as secondary.
platform.player_hardware_needed: Minimum: a 2020+ laptop with integrated graphics (Intel Iris Xe, AMD Radeon 680M/780M, Apple M1+) and 8 GB RAM, Chrome/Edge/Safari 26. Expected on iGPU (estimates, unverified until benchmarked): 30-60 fps at 1080p output with render scale 0.6-0.75 and TAAU upscaling, 2-3 shadow cascades at 2048, half-res GTAO, baked light probes, and SSGI/SSR off. On a mid-range dedicated GPU (RTX 3060/4060-class): 60+ fps at 1080p-1440p with SSGI or VXGI, SSR and higher-res shadows. Budget guidance: aim for <300-500 draw calls (use BatchedMesh/instancing), <1.5-3M visible triangles, and <1-1.5 GB GPU memory with KTX2-compressed textures.
platform.developer_hardware_needed: AI agents in this GPU-less Linux container can write all the code and run the data pipelines (Overture footprints, USGS LiDAR height extraction, texture processing, glTF/KTX2 compression via npm gltf-transform). They can also produce headless screenshots via software rendering (Chrome + SwiftShader: WebGL2 works, WebGPU via software is slow or uncertain, unverified). They cannot measure real FPS or judge final visual quality on real GPUs. The owner does NOT need a gaming PC: their normal laptop is the right test device for the student audience. A mid-range desktop GPU is only useful as an 'Ultra preset' test (optional). Running TRELLIS.2 locally would need a 24 GB NVIDIA GPU (https://huggingface.co/microsoft/TRELLIS.2-4B), so use cloud services instead.

v.multiplayer_fit: Good fit and largely independent of the rendering choice. The campus is static geometry, so Colyseus only syncs players, NPC state and mission state. The same simplified collision meshes (footprint prisms from LiDAR heights) can be loaded by Rapier on the client and, if needed, on the server. Rendering cost per extra player is small with shared, instanced character meshes. The main caution is to keep other players' avatars within the draw-call and skinning budget on iGPUs (LOD avatars, cap visible players at ~20-30). Realism effects (TAA, SSGI) cause ghosting on fast-moving avatars, which is tunable. Download size matters more in multiplayer, because friends must load the same assets before playing together, so use streaming and LOD tiers.

data_and_assets_needed: Building footprints and names: Overture buildings (already being downloaded by main session) + OSM tags for building:levels/roof:shape where present.

Accurate heights and roof shapes: USGS 3DEP 'USGS_LPC_IL_4County_Cook_2017_LAS_2019' EPT point cloud (reachable now; classified LAS incl. building/ground). Agents can compute per-building heights (building-return percentiles minus ground) and roof planes with Python (laspy/lazrs or PDAL) for the ~1.2 km x 1.0 km bbox.
Terrain/ground: same LiDAR (ground class), so the campus is effectively flat; a simple DEM is enough.

Streets, sidewalks, plazas, lawns, trees: Overture transportation/base themes + OSM (overpass is blocked; Overture S3 is reachable). Individual tree positions can be derived from LiDAR vegetation class.

Reference and texture photos from the owner: straight-on, overcast-day photos of each landmark facade (University Hall, Student Center East, Behavioral Sciences, Library, Lecture Center/Grant Hall area, SCE, Science and Engineering South, etc.), plus close-ups of concrete, brick, paving, railings, signage-free details. Roughly 300-800 photos total (estimate).

Architectural reference: floor counts, window-grid counts and setbacks for landmark buildings (from photos and public sources; e.g., University Hall 28 stories, ~103 m) to drive procedural facade generators.

CC0 materials: ambientCG/Poly Haven concrete (board-formed, precast, weathered), brick, asphalt, pavers, grass, metal and glass. Hosts blocked: owner must unblock ambientcg.com, polyhaven.com, api.polyhaven.com and dl.polyhaven.org, or download a curated pack manually.
HDRI skies: Poly Haven overcast and clear urban HDRIs (CC0), or the three.js physical SkyMesh (no download needed).
Props/vehicles/vegetation: AI-generated (Meshy/Tripo paid tier) or CC0 models; trees probably as CC0 models or procedural (ez-tree-style) with impostors for distance.
Characters/avatars: separate problem; CC0 or AI-generated rigged characters, the weakest realism area.

ai_agent_buildability.explanation: Strong parts (agents can do these well): all code (three.js r186 WebGPU/TSL ships every needed effect as built-in nodes, so no novel graphics research is required); the data pipeline (Overture + USGS LiDAR, verified reachable) to produce accurately sized and positioned massing; procedural facade generators for repetitive Brutalist grids (window modules, spandrels, columns, instancing, interior-mapping shaders for windows); texture compression (KTX2/meshopt via gltf-transform); quality presets and LOD/streaming; photo rectification scripts (OpenCV homography from 4 corner points, which pip can install). Weak parts: (1) Agents cannot see what they make at real speed. There is no GPU here, so screenshots must come from slow software rendering or from the owner. The art iteration loop ('does this look real?') depends on the owner sending screenshots and feedback, which is the main bottleneck for a realism goal. (2) Artistic judgment for grime, weathering, color grading and composition is where AAA realism comes from, and it is hard to do blind. (3) AI image-to-3D tools are not good at architecture: none of the reviewed sources benchmark buildings, and these models are tuned for object-centric assets. Use them for props only, and build buildings from data plus procedural code. (4) Performance tuning needs real devices.

v.owner_effort: 1) Take photos on campus: 1-3 afternoons on an overcast day (no harsh shadows), standing as square-on to each facade as possible, plus close-ups of materials. Avoid people, and avoid UIC logos/signage as textures. 2) Playtest every milestone on their own laptop and report FPS (agents can add an on-screen FPS counter and a 'copy device info' button). Send screenshots of things that look fake. 3) Unblock hosts for CC0 assets (ambientcg.com, polyhaven.com, api.polyhaven.com, dl.polyhaven.org), or download a curated texture list manually. Optionally unblock huggingface.co. 4) Optionally create a Meshy (or Tripo/Rodin) account. Use a paid tier (~$20/mo, or the $5.99 student plan if eligible) for 1-2 months to generate props, or accept CC BY credit on Meshy free. Do not use the Tripo free tier. 5) Approve a 'graphics preset' policy, e.g. iGPU = Medium at 30-60 fps, accepting that phones get a low-detail version. 6) Decide on credits/attribution text (OSM/Overture, AI tool credits). No software installs or gaming PC are required.
risks: Expectation gap: GTA 6 (PS5/Xbox Series, Nov 19 2026 release per secondary reports) is the product of a very large AAA studio over many years. A browser campus built by AI agents plus one non-technical owner will look clearly below it, especially at street level, with people, and with foliage. Realistic target: 'convincing architectural visualization with game lighting', roughly 2014-2016 open-world quality on good hardware.

Integrated-GPU performance: SSGI, SSR and VXGI are likely too heavy for typical student laptops. On iGPUs realism falls back to baked probes and AO, which visibly lowers lighting quality. All FPS numbers here are estimates until benchmarked on the owner's laptop.
three.js WebGPURenderer maturity: forum reports show WebGPU sometimes slower than WebGL and shadow regressions (r182), and the API changes every monthly release. Pin the version (0.186.1).
Browser coverage: Firefox on Linux and some older devices lack WebGPU, so the WebGL2 fallback path gets fewer effects.

Download size: a realistic textured campus can easily balloon past 200-500 MB. Without strict KTX2 compression, texture atlasing and streaming, first load on campus Wi-Fi becomes painful. Target ≤50-80 MB to first playable.
Agents iterate on visuals 'blind'. The realism loop depends on owner screenshots, which slows progress and risks plateauing at 'clean CG' look.

AI 3D generators produce blobby, non-orthogonal geometry for buildings, plus dense messy meshes needing retopology/decimation. Use them only for props. Free-tier license traps: Tripo retains rights on free outputs, and Meshy free requires CC BY credit.
Hunyuan3D license excludes the EU/UK/South Korea, which matters if any collaborators or players are there. Prefer MIT TRELLIS.2 or paid commercial tools.
Photo textures: de-lighting is hard. Baked-in shadows and perspective distortion from handheld photos can look worse than clean CC0 materials, and trees, cars and people occlude facades.
Data accuracy: 2017 LiDAR predates any post-2017 construction on campus. Check for newer buildings or demolitions in the bbox (e.g., recent UIC projects) against current Overture/OSM.
Scope creep: chasing realism can consume the whole project before missions exist. Timebox the 'map' milestone.
v.can_combine_with: 1) Gaussian splats for hero spots: three.js r186 has a native GaussianSplat renderer, and Spark 2.0 (MIT) adds LOD streaming. Captured splats of 1-3 signature plazas or interiors, paired with invisible collider meshes (as World Labs' Spark + Rapier demo does), give photoreal street-level patches. Splats have baked lighting, so time-of-day changes and dynamic shadows will not match. 2) Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles streamed live only as a distant Chicago skyline backdrop (tile.googleapis.com is reachable). Terms forbid caching/offline use and measurement extraction, so it cannot become game meshes. 3) LiDAR + Overture data pipeline is the foundation for any approach (game-engine or web). 4) If realism must go much higher, the same data and procedural generators can feed a native engine (Unreal 5 desktop build, or Pixel Streaming to browsers at per-player GPU server cost). Unity 6.6 WebGPU web builds reportedly support URP features but not HDRP. Babylon.js 9 (March 2026: clustered lighting, volumetric light, frame graph, splat shadows) and PlayCanvas (strong WebGPU + splat tooling) are viable alternatives with similar ceilings. Neither is clearly better for realism than three.js r186, which now has SSGI/VXGI/SSR/TAAU built in, so stay with three.js for continuity with the existing plan.
v.verdict_for_this_project: This is the recommended baseline, but expectations must be reset. It is the only approach that keeps the owner's browser + multiplayer choice, is fully buildable by AI agents in this container (data verified reachable: Overture S3, USGS Cook County LiDAR, npm three@0.186.1), costs ~$0-20/month, and produces geometrically accurate, recognizably-UIC buildings. It will not be 'close to GTA 6'. Honest target: aerial ~6/10 and street level ~4-5/10 on a typical student laptop, rising maybe 1 point on a gaming PC with SSGI/SSR. That is good-looking architectural-visualization quality, which Brutalist concrete flatters. Recommended recipe: LiDAR-accurate massing for all buildings; procedural facade generators plus CC0 concrete materials for all buildings; owner-photo-derived textures and hand-tuned detail for 5-8 landmarks (University Hall first); physical sky or HDRI, CSM shadows, GTAO, LightProbeGrid baked GI, TRAA/TAAU, bloom and ACES/AgX tone mapping as the iGPU 'Medium' preset; SSGI/VXGI + SSR as 'High'; AI generators (Meshy/Tripo paid) only for props. Build a single-building 'University Hall + plaza' realism vertical slice first. Have the owner judge it on their laptop before committing to the whole campus. If the owner finds that slice unacceptable vs their GTA 6 hopes, the realistic alternative is a native Unreal 5 desktop game, which gives up the browser and is much harder for agents, rather than further browser tricks. Possibly combine with Gaussian-splat hero spots for street-level photorealism.

v.approach: Desktop game engine (Unreal Engine 5, Unity 6 alternative)
v.one_paragraph_summary: Unreal Engine 5 (UE 5.8, released June 2026) gives the best graphics any route can offer: real-time global illumination (Lumen), very detailed geometry (Nanite), scanned concrete and asphalt materials, and realistic people (MetaHumans). It is what professional studios use for photoreal cities. It still won't get this project to "GTA 6". GTA 6 comes from a very large team with years of hand-built art and an unofficial budget reported above $1B. A non-artist working with AI agents can realistically reach "good indie UE5 game": convincing light, sky and concrete, but generic-looking buildings whose details don't match the real ones, unless someone photo-scans or hand-models each important building. Choosing UE5 also changes the project in three ways. (1) It is no longer a browser game. Players download a Windows game of several GB, or the project pays about $1–2 per player-hour to stream it from cloud GPUs (Pixel Streaming). (2) The owner needs a gaming PC (RTX-class GPU, 32 GB RAM, 1 TB+ SSD) or a rented cloud GPU workstation. The AI agents can't build, run or screenshot UE5 in today's GPU-less Linux container. They would have to run on that Windows GPU machine and work through Epic's new, experimental Unreal MCP plugin plus Python and C++. Much of UE is binary assets and Blueprints that text-only agents can't edit directly. (3) Most UIC students' laptops have integrated graphics and 8–16 GB RAM, and they can't run Lumen/Nanite at playable frame rates. Macs get only reduced features. Unity 6 is easier for AI agents (C# code, text-based YAML scenes, an official MCP server) and can export to the web via WebGPU. But its high-end renderer, HDRP, is in maintenance mode and doesn't run on the web, so Unity's web realism lands near what three.js can already do. My recommendation is to keep the browser game as the main product and push its realism as far as it can go. Treat UE5 as an optional later "high-graphics edition" or trailer tool, not a replacement.

realism.what_it_looks_like: UE5, built by AI agents and a non-artist: Lumen gives physically plausible daylight, soft shadows, bounce light and sky. Megascans-style scanned materials (board-formed concrete, asphalt, grass, brick) make surfaces look real up close. That suits East Campus, which is mostly simple Brutalist concrete masses by Walter Netsch. Agents can generate building shells from Overture/OSM footprints and heights through UE Python editor scripting and the PCG framework (production-ready in UE 5.7: https://80.lv/articles/unreal-engine-5-7-is-now-availabe). They can then apply concrete materials and window grids. The result reads as 'a realistic modern city block' in screenshots and video, roughly a solid indie UE5 game. It is not GTA 6. Hero landmarks (University Hall, Student Center East, the Quad, Daley Library) would only look like themselves if someone photo-scans them with RealityScan, which is free under $1M revenue (https://www.realityscan.com/license), or a 3D artist models them. Unity 6: on desktop, HDRP can approach UE quality with more manual work, but HDRP is now in maintenance mode (https://unity.com/topics/render-pipelines-strategy-for-2026). Unity web builds are URP-only, since HDRP is not available on WebGPU (https://discussions.unity.com/t/unity-6-hdrp-on-webgpu/1540460), so a Unity web version lands about 4/10, similar to a well-lit three.js scene. Aerial: Cesium for Unreal can stream Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles, which look very good from above or as a skyline backdrop (about 8/10). Google's terms forbid caching it and forbid building your own geometry derived from it (https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/tile/policies), so it can only be a streamed backdrop.
realism.weaknesses_up_close: 1) Generic architecture: procedural facades won't match the real window patterns, the University Hall tower's flared upper floors, the Netsch 'field theory' geometry, signage or entrances, unless each is scanned or hand-modeled. AI agents are weak at authoring detailed custom 3D meshes. 2) Google 3D Tiles look 'melted' and blocky at ground level. Cesium staff say the dataset 'doesn't necessarily provide the quality you're looking for' from a ground POV (https://community.cesium.com/t/how-can-we-improve-the-quality-to-actually-look-photorealistic-using-cesium-for-unreal/36639). 3) Interiors, props, foliage, cars and crowds all need assets. Megascans are no longer free for unlimited use since 2025 (https://80.lv/articles/megascans-no-longer-free-after-2024/). 4) Characters: MetaHumans look excellent but are heavy, and animating them believably takes skill. 5) GTA-level realism comes from thousands of hand-authored details and lighting passes, which this team doesn't have. The GTA 6 budget is unofficially reported above $1B (https://vandal.elespanol.com/en/grand-theft-auto-6/gta-6-cost-and-budget.html) (unverified).

platform.runs_in_web_browser: UE5: no. Epic removed HTML5 export years ago, and the only browser option is Pixel Streaming: the game runs on a cloud GPU and video streams to the browser. That costs about $0.53/hr (AWS g4dn.xlarge, T4) to $0.80/hr (g6.xlarge, L4) on-demand per instance (https://calculator.holori.com/aws/ec2/g4dn.xlarge/us-east-1, https://calculator.holori.com/aws/ec2/g6.xlarge/us-east-1). Lumen realistically means one player per GPU. Add video egress (my estimate: about 5–9 GB/hr at 1080p, roughly $0.45–0.80/hr at AWS internet egress rates, unverified). Total: about $1–2 per concurrent player-hour, plus latency for Chicago users. Managed services (Vagon about $0.018/min, roughly $1.08/hr: https://vagon.io/blog/best-pixel-streaming-platforms; vendor claim, unverified). Unity 6: partial. It has WebGL2 by default and WebGPU opt-in, and a secondary source says Unity 6.6 brings GPU Resident Drawer, Adaptive Probe Volumes and VFX Graph to WebGPU (https://app.cinevva.com/news/2026-09-01-unity-6-6-webgpu-production) (unverified). HDRP doesn't run on the web (https://discussions.unity.com/t/unity-6-hdrp-on-webgpu/1540460), so Unity web realism lands near a good three.js/WebGPU build.
platform.desktop: UE5: Windows is the primary target and works well. Download via Steam (Steam Direct fee $100, recouped after $1,000 in revenue: https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/gettingstarted/appfee) or itch.io (default revenue share reportedly 10% and adjustable, unverified). Install size: an empty UE5 shipping build is about 321 MB (https://www.strayspark.studio/blog/ue5-packaging-shipping-build-size-optimization). A photoreal campus with Megascans textures would plausibly be 3–15 GB (estimate, unverified). The fan-packaged City Sample was about 17–21 GB. Mac: Lumen is software-only, Nanite only on M2+ with macOS 15 (M1 unsupported), and TSR is costly on Apple Silicon (https://www.unrealengine.com/tech-blog/bringing-unreal-engine-on-macos-up-to-feature-parity-with-windowsprogress-report). Mac builds also have to be made on a Mac. Linux: possible. Unity 6: Windows, Mac and Linux desktop builds are all straightforward.
platform.phones: Not realistic for a Lumen/Nanite photoreal build. UE5 and Unity mobile builds need heavily reduced graphics, which defeats the purpose. Pixel Streaming to a phone browser works technically but costs about $1–2 per player-hour.
platform.player_hardware_needed: UE5 with Lumen and Nanite: roughly GTX 1660 for about 20 fps at 1080p with software Lumen, RTX 2060 minimum and RTX 3060 recommended for hardware Lumen (forum-posted benchmark spec, not Epic's: https://techpowerup.com/forums/goto/post?id=5335136) (unverified). UE 5.8's new 'Lumen Lite' is designed to cut GPU cost, with Epic citing 60 fps on Switch 2 and PCs (https://www.unrealengine.com/news/state-of-unreal-2026-top-news-from-the-show). That helps mid-range GPUs, but integrated laptop graphics are still a stretch. Epic itself recommends DX11 for laptops with integrated graphics, which means no Nanite or Lumen (https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/unreal-engine/hardware-and-software-specifications-for-unreal-engine). Typical UIC student laptops: UIC department guides recommend Intel i5/i7 or Apple M1–M3 with 8–16 GB RAM and no discrete GPU (https://law.uic.edu/student-support/its/computer-buying-guide, https://dentistry.uic.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/741/2025/08/UIC-Dentistry-Laptop-Requirements-08-2025.pdf). Honest conclusion: most UIC students could NOT play a photoreal UE5 build at acceptable frame rates. Only students with gaming laptops or desktops (RTX 3060/4060-class, the most common Steam GPUs in 2026: https://www.digitalcitizen.life/nvidia-rtx-5070-most-popular-gpu-steam-hardware-survey-september-2026/) could. Everyone else would need a much-reduced 'low' mode or Pixel Streaming.
platform.developer_hardware_needed: UE5 editor: Epic recommends Windows 11, a quad-core 2.5 GHz+ CPU, 32 GB RAM and a DX12 GPU with 8 GB+ VRAM. Workarounds exist: Edgegap's prebuilt images (https://docs.edgegap.com/unreal-engine), or listen-server mode where one player hosts, at $0. Hosting: Edgegap charges about $0.069 per vCPU-hour, or a 'Hobbyist' 1 vCPU/2 GB server at about $22/month running 24/7, plus $0.10/GB egress (https://edgegap.com/pricing, https://edgegap.com/blog/announcement-offering-changes-for-2025). Epic Online Services (lobbies, P2P relay) is free (unverified this session). Pixel Streaming multiplayer works, but each viewer needs their own GPU instance (about $1–2/player-hour). Unity 6: Netcode for GameObjects is free. Unity Relay gives the first 50 average monthly CCU free, then $0.16 per CCU (https://unity.com/products/gaming-services/pricing). A third-party blog says Unity's Multiplay hosting was wound down in early 2026 (https://crux.supercraft.host/blog/unity-gaming-services-alternatives/) (unverified), so dedicated servers would go to Edgegap or a plain VPS. Both engines handle 2–50 player campus sessions fine technically. Multiplayer isn't the blocker: the cost of streaming, and players' hardware, are.

ai_agent_buildability.explanation: In THIS environment, UE5 scores 1/10: no GPU, 15 GB RAM against Epic's 32 GB recommendation, about 30 GB free disk, engine downloads blocked, and Epic container images gated behind an Epic-linked GitHub token. Agents can't compile, cook, run or screenshot anything. On a Windows RTX machine with Claude Code installed locally, UE5 rises to about 5/10. Agents can write C++ gameplay code as text. They can automate the editor with Python (editor-only, not a runtime scripting language: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/scripting-the-unreal-editor-using-python). For example, they can import Overture/OSM footprints, spawn and extrude buildings, assign materials, and set up PCG graphs. They can also drive the editor through Epic's experimental Unreal MCP plugin (spawn actors, lighting, material instances, automation tests) or community MCP servers that offer viewport screenshots (https://www.strayspark.studio/blog/epic-official-mcp-plugin-ue5-8-vs-third-party). They can't diff or merge .uasset/.umap binaries or Blueprint graphs as text. MCP coverage is described as 'incomplete', so some steps (material tweaking, lighting art direction, fixing editor dialogs, Fab/Bridge downloads) will fall to the owner clicking in the editor. Builds are slow (shader compiles, cooking), and Git needs LFS for multi-GB assets. Unity 6 scores about 5/10 here and 6/10 on a GPU machine. C# is text, scenes and prefabs can be Force-Text YAML (https://docs.unity.com/en-us/engine/6000.3/manual/working-with-scenes/text-scene-format.md), and there is an official Unity MCP (https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.ai.assistant@2.0/manual/unity-mcp-overview.html). Batchmode works without a GPU but can't render. Unity downloads and licensing hosts are also blocked here. Compare three.js in this container: agents can build, run headless Chromium with software WebGL and screenshot-test today, which is about 9/10.

v.owner_effort: For UE5, a lot more than the current plan. 1) Buy or rent a Windows gaming PC (RTX 4070-class, 32–64 GB RAM, 2 TB SSD), or set up a cloud GPU workstation with remote desktop and remember to shut it down. 2) Create an Epic Games account and install the Epic Launcher plus UE 5.8 (50–100 GB). For dedicated servers or container images, link GitHub to Epic and possibly build the engine from source. 3) Install Claude Code (and Git LFS) on that PC, and approve many permission prompts. 4) Enable Unreal MCP/AllToolsets plugins, open the editor so agents can drive it, and sometimes click through dialogs, Fab downloads, material or lighting tweaks the agents can't reach. Expect a few hours a week inside the editor. 5) Buy and download Fab/Megascans assets with the Epic account. 6) For buildings that look like the real ones: walk campus taking 100–300 overlapping photos per landmark facade and run RealityScan, or hire a 3D artist (unverified cost; likely hundreds to thousands of dollars per hero building). 7) Playtest locally, and decide between Steam/itch downloads and paying for Pixel Streaming. Unity has a similar hardware need, plus a Unity account and license activation.
risks: Expectation gap: 'GTA 6 graphics' isn't reachable by any route with this team. UE5 gets closest, but a non-artist with AI agents will produce generic photoreal buildings, not accurate UIC replicas, unless the owner photo-scans or hires an artist.

AI agents lose their current superpower: they can't run, test or screenshot UE5 in the GPU-less container. Every iteration needs the owner's GPU machine to be on, and the owner becomes the bottleneck and an editor operator.
Audience loss: most UIC student laptops (integrated graphics, 8–16 GB RAM, many Macs) can't run Lumen/Nanite at playable FPS, and 'open a link and play' becomes 'download several GB on a gaming PC'.
Pixel Streaming costs scale per player (~$1–2/player-hour). That's far above the current ~$10–15/month server, and needs autoscaling and budget alerts to avoid surprise bills.
Unreal MCP is experimental, with changing APIs and no auth, and Blueprint/.uasset binaries can't be reviewed or merged in Git. Expect breakage and harder code review.
Engine churn: UE 5.8 is the last planned UE5. UE6 Early Access is targeted for end-2027, with possible migration work and possible Blueprint deprecation (unverified).
Asset costs and licensing: Megascans are no longer free, every paid asset's Fab license tier needs tracking, and Google 3D Tiles can only be a streamed backdrop (no caching or derived geometry).
Disk and repo bloat: projects reach tens to hundreds of GB and need Git LFS, which strains GitHub free LFS quotas (unverified specifics).

v.can_combine_with: 1) Best hybrid, which I recommend: keep the browser game (three.js/WebGPU + Colyseus) as the real, playable multiplayer product and raise its realism with PBR concrete materials, baked or real-time lighting, HDR sky, accurate Overture/OSM footprints and heights, per-building facade textures from the owner's own photos, and RealityScan-captured hero landmarks exported as glTF. The same glTF/photogrammetry assets can later be reused in UE5. 2) UE5 as a showcase or trailer tool: one cloud-GPU session renders cinematic trailers and screenshots of the campus with Lumen and Movie Render Queue for marketing, while the game stays in the browser. 3) An optional 'High-Graphics Edition': a later downloadable UE5 Windows build sharing the same data pipeline (footprints JSON + scanned meshes) and possibly the same mission logic and server protocol, for students with gaming PCs. 4) Cesium for Unreal + Google 3D Tiles as a distant streamed skyline (Loop towers, Sears/Willis) behind our own modeled campus, subject to the tiles' attribution/no-caching terms. Cesium also has a CesiumJS/three.js path for the web route. 5) Pixel Streaming as a 'try it in your browser' demo for a few concurrent users only.
v.verdict_for_this_project: Not recommended as the main route right now, but worth keeping as a later add-on. UE5 gives the highest realism ceiling, about 6/10 at street level for this team against a GTA-6 10. It isn't 10, because accuracy of the real buildings comes from photo capture and art time, not from the engine. To get that extra realism, the project would give up all three things that make the current plan work: (a) AI agents building and testing autonomously in the container, (b) a $0 setup with no gaming PC for the owner, and (c) classmates playing instantly on ordinary laptops in a browser, with multiplayer that's cheap to host. Unity 6 doesn't fix this: its web output can't use HDRP, so its browser realism is close to three.js, and its desktop path has the same hardware and testing problems. If the owner insists that realism outranks reach and is willing to (1) spend about $1.5–2.5k on a Windows RTX PC or about $100/month on a cloud GPU, (2) spend several hours a week clicking in the editor, and (3) accept that only gaming-PC owners can play locally (others via Pixel Streaming at about $1–2 per player-hour), then UE 5.8 + Claude Code on that PC + Epic's Unreal MCP + Python-generated buildings from Overture data + Megascans concrete + RealityScan hero buildings is the right stack. Unity is the fallback only if the agents' C#/YAML editing matters more than visual ceiling. Otherwise: maximize browser realism now, capture real facades with phone photos, and revisit a UE5 'High-Graphics Edition' after Milestone 3 once the gameplay is proven. Hosts to unblock if the owner wants agents to try Unity here anyway: download.unity3d.com, public-cdn.cloud.unity3d.com and Unity's licensing hosts (exact list unverified). It would still have no GPU. Unblocking www.unrealengine.com alone wouldn't make UE5 runnable here, because of RAM, disk and GPU limits.

v.approach: Captured photoreal (Gaussian splatting / photogrammetry of real buildings)
v.one_paragraph_summary: The owner walks around UIC with a phone (or a 360 camera) and films or photographs real buildings. Software turns those images into a 3D "Gaussian splat": millions of tiny colored blobs that, from the right angles, look almost like a photograph you can walk through. The splats load in the browser game through Spark, an open-source three.js library from World Labs. Spark fits the existing three.js + Rapier + Colyseus plan, and World Labs ships a three.js + Rapier third-person-controller template built on it. Hero landmarks such as University Hall, Daley Library, Student Center East and the Quad can look more "real" in a still screenshot than hand-modeled buildings. The limits show up when you play: lighting is baked in from capture day, so there is no day/night cycle and no real shadows from moving characters. Close up and in motion you get soft or blurry detail and floating "ghost" blobs. Anything the camera never saw is a hole, including roofs, the upper floors of the 103 m tower, and the backs of buildings. Splats also have no physical surfaces, so walls and floors need separate invisible collision meshes, which can be built from building footprints. Capturing all of the East Campus core is weeks of the owner's own work, best done on matching overcast days. Recommendation: use it as a hero-landmark add-on layered over a modeled or mesh campus, not as the main world-building approach.

realism.what_it_looks_like: Within the captured 'sweet spot' (eye level, along paths the owner actually walked), a well-captured splat of a matte Brutalist concrete facade looks close to a photo or video. It shows the real stains, weathering, signage and trees, which a hand-modeled game asset rarely matches. Netsch's board-formed concrete is matte and full of texture, which suits splats and photogrammetry. Glass curtain walls and reflective surfaces do not (SketchUp guide: https://help.sketchup.com/it/gaussian-splats-best-practices). The look is 'photographic diorama', not GTA 6: GTA 6 gets its realism from dynamic lighting, wet roads, reflections, time of day and dense animated life, and splats cannot do any of those. Hero spots could rate 7 to 8 in still screenshots, but the whole moving game experience is about 5 to 6. A campus captured only from the ground looks bad from the air: roofs and upper facades are missing or smeared, unless a drone is used, and drones are legally hard here (see legal).
realism.weaknesses_up_close: (1) Baked lighting. Shadows and sun direction are fixed from capture day. Splats do not receive shadows from mesh characters without proxy-mesh tricks. A day/night cycle is not realistic: PlayCanvas's proxy-mesh relighting can add a sun, point lights or an environment swap (https://developer.playcanvas.com/user-manual/gaussian-splatting/building/relighting/), but the Godot GDGS docs note that relighting is only a modulation and cannot remove shadows baked in at capture (https://radiancefields.com/reconworldlab-adds-relighting-to-godot-gaussian-splats-in-gdgs-3.3.0). (2) Floaters and ghosts from people, cars and swaying foliage; sort-order popping or flicker while the camera moves; and blur or low-res detail very close to surfaces (https://tomshardware.com/software/programming/developer-creates-a-basic-first-person-shooter-game-using-gaussian-splats-and-you-can-play-it-for-free-in-your-browser, https://www.strayspark.studio/blog/gaussian-splatting-unreal-engine-5-capture-to-game-pipeline). (3) Coverage holes. Roofs, building backs and courtyards the owner did not walk are missing. University Hall's upper roughly 70 m will be soft or holey from ground capture. Ground and pavement often degrade under a lower or downward-looking third-person camera. (4) No geometry. Collision needs proxy meshes, either extruded from footprints or generated by splat-transform's voxel/--collision-mesh option (https://developer.playcanvas.com/user-manual/splat-transform/collision/). (5) Seams. Splats captured on different days have different light and season (Chicago trees change colour and drop leaves), and those differences show where captures meet. (6) Mesh characters composited into splats tend to look 'pasted in' because they are lit by engine lights and the splats are not.

platform.runs_in_web_browser: Yes for rendering, with streaming. Spark 2.3.1 (npm @sparkjsdev/spark, published 2026-10-01, MIT) has a streamed LoD system with a capped per-frame splat budget. The defaults in its shipped TypeScript types are 2.5M splats on desktop, 1 to 1.5M on mobile and 500K to 750K in WebXR, with paged chunk fetching through 4 web workers (verified in the package's SparkRenderer.d.ts). Spark's docs suggest roughly 1 to 5M splats on typical computers (https://sparkjs.dev/docs/performance/). PlayCanvas engine 2.23.2 and splat-transform 3.10.1 (both MIT, published Oct 2026) offer Streamed SOG LOD. PlayCanvas reports 35M splats at 76 fps with its new WebGPU renderer versus 13 fps on WebGL2 (vendor claim, hardware unstated: https://blog.playcanvas.com/new-in-supersplat-webgpu-and-streaming-bring-huge-performance-wins). three.js r186 now ships an examples/jsm/objects/GaussianSplat.js addon plus SPZ, KSPLAT and glTF splat loaders. That addon is WebGPURenderer-only and has no LoD (verified in the three@0.186.1 package). mkkellogg GaussianSplats3D is officially no longer in active development; its README recommends Spark.
platform.desktop: Works in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari via WebGL2 (Spark targets 98%+ of devices per its README). No independent browser benchmark on Intel Iris or integrated GPUs was found. One proxy figure is a native (non-browser) RViz plugin: about 20 fps for a 6M-splat scene on a modern iGPU and 100+ fps at 1 to 3M (https://discourse.openrobotics.org/t/rvizsplat-visualize-3d-gaussian-splats-in-rviz/54487). Expect iGPU laptops to need about 1 to 1.5M splats on screen plus simple mesh characters (estimate, unverified).
platform.phones: Partial. Spark auto-reduces its budget to 1 to 1.5M on mobile. Viewing works, but a full game plus multiplayer plus splats on phones will look softer and run hotter (unverified for this scene).
platform.player_hardware_needed: Any laptop from about 2020 on with WebGL2. A discrete GPU helps but is not required, because LoD caps the work. Download size is significant: hundreds of MB for a campus, streamed progressively (estimate, unverified).
platform.developer_hardware_needed: AI agents in a GPU-less Linux container CAN write the Spark/three.js/Rapier game code. They can also convert, compress, crop and LOD-build splats with splat-transform: most operations run on CPU via '--gpu cpu', though GPU-only filters such as --filter-cluster do not (splat-transform README, verified). Agents CANNOT practically train splats: gsplat and nerfstudio need CUDA, and OpenSplat on CPU is about 100x slower (https://github.com/pierotofy/OpenSplat). COLMAP pose estimation on CPU is possible but slow. Agents also cannot visually judge quality without a GPU. Training has to happen on (a) the phone itself (Scaniverse, on-device and free), (b) a vendor cloud (Polycam, KIRI, Luma), (c) the owner's computer running Brush (Apache-2.0; runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, AMD/NVIDIA/Intel GPUs, Android and in Chrome via WebGPU, per its README), or (d) a rented cloud GPU. Postshot and RealityScan desktop want an NVIDIA RTX-class GPU (https://jawset.com, https://www.realityscan.com/en-US/download). A gaming PC is not strictly required, but an RTX PC or rented GPU makes quality iteration much faster.

v.multiplayer_fit: Good, because splats are static scenery. Every player streams the same splat chunks from a CDN, and Colyseus only syncs players and missions, exactly as with mesh scenery. Proof point: STARSPEED is a browser multiplayer game using Spark-streamed splats with Colyseus (https://www.worldlabs.ai/labs/showcase/starspeed). Server-side physics needs the proxy collision meshes (footprint extrusions), which are tiny and deterministic, and the server never needs the splats. One limitation: other players' avatars are lit by engine lights while the splat world has baked light, so characters can look composited. Use a fixed time of day matching the capture (overcast) and a ground shadow-catcher mesh for character shadows (technique, unverified for Spark specifically).

legal_and_licensing.finding: The copyright in a constructed architectural work does not include the right to prevent making, distributing or publicly displaying pictures, paintings, photographs or other pictorial representations of the work if the building is located in or ordinarily visible from a public place. Courts have not clearly settled whether a 3D splat or mesh is a 'pictorial representation' (no case found; unverified). That uncertainty mostly does not matter here: per the Copyright Office's Circular 41, architectural-works copyright only covers buildings created on or after Dec 1, 1990, and Netsch's 1960s East Campus buildings (University Hall, Daley Library, Student Center East) predate it. Post-1990 UIC buildings rely on §120(a).

legal_and_licensing.topic: AWCPA 1990 cutoff (pre-1990 buildings unprotected as architectural works)
legal_and_licensing.finding: Copyright protects architectural works created on or after Dec 1, 1990, plus designs unbuilt but in unpublished plans on that date and constructed by Dec 31, 2002. Individual sculptures or artworks on campus could have their own copyright (unverified per item).

legal_and_licensing.topic: UIC campus photography policy and trademarks
legal_and_licensing.finding: UIC guidelines: outdoor photography within the public domain is permitted. Shooting inside facilities needs authorization from Strategic Marketing and Communications (SMC). Professional or commercial photographers need SMC written permission to reproduce images of the university, including its name, recognizable landmarks or buildings. Commercial shoots need 3 weeks' notice, insurance and fees. Photographing individuals without consent is prohibited, and minors need guardian consent. Practical reading: a student capturing building exteriors from walkways is fine. Before publishing a public game that shows UIC buildings, names or logos, email SMC (University Hall, 13th floor) for written OK, which also covers the separate trademark issue. Whether §120(a) overrides UIC's 'permission to reproduce buildings' language is a legal question that was not verified.

legal_and_licensing.topic: People, faces, license plates in captures
legal_and_licensing.finding: Remove or blur people and plates before training. Meta's EgoBlur (Apache-2.0; face and license-plate detector with Gaussian blur, CLI for images and video, pip 'egoblur') can pre-blur frames. Brush supports per-image masks to ignore regions during training. Remaining 'ghost' people can be deleted in SuperSplat (MIT). Capture at low-traffic times (early weekend mornings, breaks). Illinois BIPA covers 'scans of face geometry'. N.D. Ill. courts have held that face geometry derived from photos can fall under BIPA despite the photo exclusion. Splat training is not facial recognition, so risk is low (unverified), but pre-blurring removes it.

ai_agent_buildability.explanation: The code side is very agent-friendly. Spark is an npm three.js library with typed APIs, and the existing plan's stack (three.js + Rapier + Colyseus) matches World Labs' open-source third-person controller and STARSPEED exactly. Agents can also script the asset pipeline on CPU: splat-transform format conversion, cropping, SOG/SPZ/LOD output and collision voxels; COLMAP; EgoBlur face/plate blurring on CPU (slow); and extruding footprint collision meshes from the Overture data already being downloaded. What agents cannot do in this container: train splats (no GPU), look at the result and judge 'does this look real', or capture anything. Quality iteration is a human-in-the-loop job: the owner captures, someone with a GPU trains, the owner walks it in SuperSplat or the game and reports problems. Aligning several splats to real-world coordinates and to the footprint collision meshes is fiddly but scriptable.

data_and_assets_needed: Phone video or photos of each hero building: 2 to 3 slow loops at different heights or angles plus close facade passes. Typically several hundred to about 1,000+ frames per building. Overlap of 70 to 80% (https://help.sketchup.com/it/gaussian-splats-best-practices). Polycam caps splats at 1,000 images per capture.
Captures taken in consistent overcast light, in one season, at low-traffic times (people and cars cause floaters)
Building footprints and heights (Overture, already being downloaded) for proxy collision meshes and for georeferencing splats
A GPU-equipped trainer: phone on-device (Scaniverse), vendor cloud (Polycam, KIRI), the owner's laptop running Brush, or a rented GPU
Face and license-plate blur pass (EgoBlur) or masks before training
Modeled or mesh filler for everything not captured: roofs, non-hero buildings, roads, terrain, trees. This comes from the other researchers' approaches.
Ground shadow-catcher meshes and a fixed lighting setup matching capture conditions
Optional: written OK from UIC SMC before public release
v.owner_effort: This approach is the most owner-labor-heavy option, because only someone physically on campus can capture. (1) Learn capture technique: about 2 to 4 hours of practice, for example testing Scaniverse (free, on-device) on one small building and walking the result in SuperSplat. (2) Per hero building: about 45 to 90 minutes on site for a full loop at 2 to 3 heights plus facade detail (my estimate from capture-guide overlap rules; unverified). University Hall's 28-story tower cannot be covered above the lower floors from the ground. (3) Whole East Campus core, about 15 to 25 buildings plus the Quad and walkways: roughly 25 to 50 hours of capture spread over several weeks, constrained to overcast days in a single season and low-traffic times. Some re-shoots are inevitable (estimate, unverified). (4) Choose and maybe pay for a processing route, or provide or rent a GPU. (5) Playtest-review each splat for holes and floaters. (6) Email UIC SMC for permission before public launch. A hero-landmarks-only scope (4 to 6 sites) is about 8 to 15 hours of capture, which is realistic for a student.
risks: Realism ceiling: baked lighting, no day/night, characters that look composited, and blur close up. The result reads as a 'photographic diorama', not GTA 6. The owner may be disappointed in motion even if screenshots look amazing.
Coverage holes: roofs, the University Hall tower top, building backs and service areas will be missing or smeared without a drone, and a drone is legally impractical at UIC and in Chicago.
Inconsistency across captures: weather, sun angle, season and foliage changes produce visible seams between splats and against modeled filler.
Labor bottleneck on the owner: capture cannot be delegated to AI agents, and quality iteration needs GPU training outside this container.

Licensing traps: Scaniverse Free/Plus and Postshot Free do not grant commercial rights. The original Inria 3DGS code is non-commercial. Avoid those for anything that might be monetized, and use COLMAP (BSD) + Brush or gsplat (Apache).
Privacy: people and plates in frames. UIC prohibits photographing individuals without consent, and there is a BIPA edge risk. This requires a blur or mask step and capture at quiet times.

Ecosystem churn: Spark's owner World Labs is being acquired by AMD (announced Sept 28, 2026). GaussianSplats3D is already abandoned. Luma has pivoted to video. Formats are still moving (SPZ v4, .RAD, Streamed SOG, Khronos glTF splat extensions).
Performance and download size on integrated-GPU laptops when several hero splats plus a mesh world plus multiplayer avatars are on screen. No direct browser iGPU benchmark was found.
UIC SMC could deny or condition permission for a public game depicting campus buildings and names.
v.can_combine_with: Best as a layer on top of a mesh-based campus. (a) Procedural or modeled buildings from Overture footprints for the whole map, with splats swapped in only for hero landmarks when the player is near; Spark renders splats and three.js meshes in one pipeline. (b) Photogrammetry meshes (RealityScan, or KIRI 3DGS-to-mesh) of the same captures, used as the proxy and collision mesh, as a shadow-receiving or relighting proxy, and as the far-LOD version. Captured facade photos can also become textures for modeled buildings, so captures improve modeled buildings without splat downsides. (c) Photorealistic 3D tile or aerial mesh sources (another researcher's area) to fill roofs and the tower top that ground capture misses, subject to their own terms. (d) Footprint-extruded collision meshes for Rapier on both client and Colyseus server. (e) A fixed overcast time-of-day lighting setup for the mesh world so it matches the splats.
v.verdict_for_this_project: Use it as a hero-landmark add-on, not as the main approach. Captured splats are the only approach here that can make University Hall, Daley Library, Student Center East and the Quad look exactly like real life at street level. The tech now fits the existing browser plan: Spark 2.x is MIT-licensed with streamed LoD, ships a three.js + Rapier character template, and STARSPEED already pairs it with Colyseus. As the main approach for the whole East Campus it fails the owner's 'GTA 6' goal in the ways that matter in play. There is no dynamic lighting or day/night, roofs and the tower top are missing without a drone (and drones are effectively barred here), splats taken on different days show visible seams, and there are weeks of owner-only capture labor. Suggested plan: (1) build the whole map as a modeled or mesh campus from Overture footprints at a fixed overcast time of day; (2) run a cheap 1-week pilot in which the owner captures one hero site (for example the Daley Library facade and plaza) with Scaniverse (free, on-device) or a raw phone video processed through COLMAP + Brush; (3) agents drop it into the three.js scene with Spark and a footprint collision proxy, and the owner walks it at street level and decides. If the pilot impresses, expand to 4 to 6 landmarks. Use an open-source or commercially licensed pipeline from the start, blur faces and plates, and ask UIC SMC before public release.

v.score_challenges:
Street-level score 3/10 is slightly inflated against the owner's 'GTA 6 / buildings look real up close' bar. Cesium staff confirm that the API serves one LOD below Google Earth ('Google Earth allows a higher maximum level of detail ... limitation of the data itself'), so street level is worse than what the owner sees in Google Earth. Lighting is baked, and there are no PBR materials, no night and no weather. Adjusted: 2/10.

Aerial 8/10 is fair to slightly high (7 to 8) for the same LOD reason and the baked lighting. It is fine for skyline and fly-over.

AI buildability 7/10 holds for a viewer, which agents can build in a day. It is inflated for a playable world on this data. Collision must come from separate data. Raycasting the tiles is a 'programmatically reading measurements' risk. There is no GPU or browser in the container for visual QA. Every test is billed. Content drifts. Legal questions need a human. Adjusted: 6/10 for the backdrop role, and about 4/10 if used as the walkable world.

The report's verdict (do not use as the main walkable world; at most a skyline or backdrop layer) is sound and, if anything, should be stronger. Even the backdrop role is legally exposed under 3.2.3(e) once owned, OSM- or Overture-based geometry sits next to it, and Section 5.2(d) allows immediate suspension for Section 3.2 violations.
missed_issues: The API is lower resolution than Google Earth. Cesium staff say the finest Google Earth LOD is not in the Photorealistic 3D Tiles dataset, and new buildings reach Google Earth before the API. So 'it looks like Google Earth' oversells it (https://community.cesium.com/t/google-tiles-in-cesium-less-detailed-than-google-earth/26721).

Immediate suspension risk. ToS 5.2(d) lets Google 'immediately Suspend' for any Section 3.2 violation (caching, scraping, creating content, non-Google-map use). The report cited only the 24-hour AUP path. If the hybrid is judged a violation, the game world disappears instantly.

AI/ML clause 3.2.3(c)(vii): Google Maps Content may not be used to 'train, test, validate or fine-tune' AI models. Agent visual QA that sends tile screenshots to AI services should be checked against the AI provider's data-use terms (probably fine for inference only; unverified).

Re-creating Google products, 3.2.3(d). Google Earth launched a browser Flight Simulator on June 12, 2026. A free 'fly-over/tour' mode over Google tiles, which the report recommends as the safest use, is the feature most likely to be seen as re-creating Google Earth.

The FAQ ban covers 'programmatically' reading and recording measurements. Game code that samples ground height every frame is literally programmatic reading. Hand-tuning an Overture collision world or hero-building placement to match the Google mesh is also arguably 'derived' content.

The quota figure may be stale. A May 2026 release note says the Photorealistic 3D quota was 'significantly increased'. The owner should read the live quota in the Cloud Console rather than plan around 10,000 per day.

Each page refresh is a new billed root request (the root response is not cacheable, per Cesium community posts). Reload-heavy dev and test loops by agents and the owner can cost more than player traffic. Set a hard daily quota cap.
Streamers and videos: attribution must stay visible in recordings. Player streams on Twitch or YouTube are not explicitly addressed (unverified).

No GPU and no headless browser installed in this container. Agents cannot currently see what they build. A Playwright Chromium download, and possibly a host allowlist, would be needed, and software-rendered photogrammetry streaming may be impractically slow.

Better alternative for the stated goal: owned assets. That means custom PBR models of University Hall and the Netsch buildings from the owner's own photos and photogrammetry. RealityScan is free for individuals, students and businesses under $1M revenue (https://www.realityscan.com/license). Add Fab/Megascans materials (a free subset; most Megascans have been paid since 2025: https://80.lv/articles/megascans-no-longer-free-after-2024/), rendered with dynamic lighting. GTA-6-adjacent visuals realistically require a native engine (Unreal Engine 5 with Lumen/Nanite), not a browser. Even in the browser, owned PBR models beat Google tiles at eye level.

Another alternative: Gaussian-splat captures of key campus spots shot on the owner's phone look photoreal at eye level and are fully owned, but they also have baked lighting and need separate collision. Worth a separate evaluation (unverified for this project).
Chicago/UIC coverage and current imagery date were never checked. Load the area once with a key, or use Google Earth's 3D coverage layer (which may differ from the API dataset).
