v.approach: Ground-truth data sources + honest GTA 6 benchmark
v.one_paragraph_summary: Getting the shape of the campus right is mostly solved, and it is free. From this container I downloaded the US government's public-domain laser scan of Chicago (USGS 3DEP LiDAR, flown April–May 2017) for the whole UIC East Campus bounding box. That is 13.3 million points at reduced depth, about 31 points per square metre at full depth. I matched it against the City of Chicago's MIT-licensed building outlines and measured every building's real height. University Hall comes out at 104.3 m against the published 103 m, and Science & Engineering Offices at 49.6 m (13 stories). This gives AI agents exact footprints, heights, roof shapes and even tree positions. What the data cannot give is how the walls look up close: the textures, windows, concrete stains and brick. That is what makes a game look 'real', and no free dataset supplies it legally. Google Street View, Google Earth and Google 3D imagery may be used only as visual reference, never copied into the game. Wikimedia Commons and Mapillary photos are legally usable with attribution and share-alike, but they are poor raw textures. The owner's own photos plus free CC0 concrete and brick materials are the best path. On the benchmark: GTA 6 is the product of a studio of thousands, roughly a decade of work and a budget analysts put in the billions. A small AI-built team cannot match it at street level on any platform. A well-lit, accurately shaped, photo-referenced campus is achievable: roughly 'good indie / 2015-era AAA' on desktop Unreal Engine 5, and 'nice architectural-visualization website' in a browser.

realism.what_it_looks_like: This approach is the data foundation, not a renderer. On its own (LiDAR plus footprints extruded and lightly textured) it gives a dimensionally exact campus: right heights, setbacks, cantilevers, rooftop mechanical units and tree canopy positions. Seen from above it reads as clearly 'UIC'. Its look depends on what is layered on top. In a browser (three.js) with good lighting and CC0 concrete and brick materials it looks like a good architectural visualization (about 4/10 at street level). In Unreal Engine 5 with Lumen lighting, Nanite meshes, hand-modelled hero buildings and the owner's photos as reference, a small team can plausibly reach about 6/10 at street level (unverified estimate). GTA 6 is the 10/10 reference.
realism.weaknesses_up_close: LiDAR samples roofs densely and walls very sparsely, so it gives no window grids, mullions, recessed window depth, board-formed concrete texture, weathering streaks or ground-floor detail; all of these must be modelled by hand or procedurally. The scan is from spring 2017 (leaf-off), so buildings finished or demolished after that are wrong or missing, and Overture or current city footprints must patch them. Classification is unreliable on this dataset: most of University Hall's points are labelled 'high vegetation' (class 5) rather than 'building' (class 6), so building/tree separation should use the footprints, not the LiDAR classes. The Chicago footprint copy that is reachable dates from about 2015; only about 29% of its 869 footprints in the bbox have a STORIES value. A 1 m DSM hillshade I rendered shows trees and roof equipment clearly, but every facade would still look like a flat textured box unless an artist or agent adds detail.

platform.runs_in_web_browser: Yes for the data. Processed footprints, heights and roof meshes become small static files (a few MB as glTF/GeoJSON) that three.js loads easily. The 534 MB raw point array is a build-time input only and is never shipped. Browser realism is capped by WebGL/WebGPU lighting; see verdict.
platform.desktop: Yes. The same derived data imports into Unreal Engine 5 (for example via Datasmith/glTF or Cesium for Unreal) or Unity HDRP. Desktop UE5 is where this data can look most real, because of Lumen global illumination and Nanite geometry.
platform.phones: Data is fine for phones once simplified. Realism on phones is far lower on any engine.
platform.player_hardware_needed: For the browser build, any recent laptop. For a UE5 desktop build aimed at high realism, a mid-range or better gaming GPU (RTX 3060-class or better is typical for Lumen; unverified exact minimum).
platform.developer_hardware_needed: Data pipeline: none. I ran all of it in this GPU-less Linux container with pip-installed laspy 2.7.0 + lazrs, shapely, pyproj and pyshp. An open3d 0.20.0 wheel is pip-downloadable. PDAL's Python package on PyPI is source-only (needs the C++ libpdal), but conda-forge is reachable, so micromamba could install it (not tested). Rendering: three.js can be built and headless-tested here. UE5 cannot realistically be run or tested in a GPU-less container. The owner would need a Windows gaming PC (or a cloud GPU machine) to open the editor and to playtest, and UE5 Blueprints and levels are binary assets that AI agents edit poorly.

v.multiplayer_fit: Neutral to good. Ground-truth geometry is static, so every player gets the same files and the server only syncs players and missions. Exact real-world scale (the derived meshes should be in metres in a local tangent frame, NOT raw EPSG:3857, where horizontal distances are inflated about 1.34x at Chicago's latitude) keeps the physics and collision consistent for Colyseus/Rapier. The data choice does not constrain multiplayer. The renderer choice does: UE5 has built-in replication, while three.js uses the existing Colyseus plan.

legal_and_licensing.topic: Cook County LiDAR dataset actually covering UIC
legal_and_licensing.finding: The only EPT dataset covering UIC is USGS_LPC_IL_4County_Cook_2017_LAS_2019 (93.7 billion points, EPSG:3857, Z in metres). It is a QL1 project collected April–May 2017, leaf-off, nominal pulse spacing 0.35 m, and was captured with Geiger-mode LiDAR. I measured about 31.6 pts/m² (all returns) around University Hall and 11.5 pts/m² over the full bbox at octree depth ≤10. The IL_8County_* datasets in the bucket do NOT cover Chicago (I checked their bounds).

USGS describes a Geiger-mode 3DEP point cloud over Chicago from project 'IL 4County Cook 2017' and labels it public domain. NOAA InPort lists the 2017 USGS Lidar Northeast IL 4 County (Cook, Kane, Lake, McHenry) metadata.

legal_and_licensing.topic: Google Maps Platform (Street View, satellite, 45° imagery, 3D tiles): reference-only
legal_and_licensing.finding: The current GMP Terms (last modified Aug 26, 2026) prohibit creating content from Google Maps Content. They give examples such as tracing building outlines from satellite and creating 3D building models from 45° imagery. They also bar bulk downloading of Street View images, caching, and using Google Maps Content to train or fine-tune AI models. So Street View, Google Earth and Google 3D imagery cannot be turned into textures or models for the game. Looking at them as a human reference while an artist builds an original model is the usual practice, but whether that is safe is my interpretation, not legal advice (unverified).

Mapillary's help center states images are shared under CC BY-SA (4.0). They can legally be used, even commercially, as textures or reference with attribution, and adaptations must be shared alike. Separate commercial/API terms also exist. Coverage around UIC is unknown, and mapillary.com and its API are blocked here.

Commons photos are individually licensed (CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA or public domain). A texture cut from a CC BY-SA photo needs attribution and must stay under CC BY-SA. Whether share-alike reaches the whole game is debated. I could not check Commons (blocked, and the search budget ran out), so licensing details are from general knowledge (unverified). Practical note: tourist photos are in perspective with baked lighting and are poor raw textures.

legal_and_licensing.topic: Photographing/recreating real buildings (US freedom of panorama)
legal_and_licensing.finding: 17 U.S.C. §120(a) lets anyone make pictures and 'pictorial representations' of an architectural work visible from a public place, so the owner's own photos of UIC buildings and a 3D game recreation are generally fine under US copyright. Trademarks (UIC name, logos, 'Flames', Sparky) are a separate issue already covered in campus-research.md. Statute text not re-fetched this session (unverified).

The owner holds full copyright, with no attribution or share-alike obligations. This is the cleanest source of facade textures and photogrammetry. Photographing UIC interiors may need university permission (unverified).

ai_agent_buildability.explanation: I proved it in this container. An agent with no GPU fetched the EPT octree over plain HTTPS and decoded LAZ with pip-installed laspy+lazrs. It fetched the whole bbox (13.3M points, about 4 minutes), joined the points to footprints with shapely/pyproj, and produced per-building heights (858 footprints) plus a 1 m DSM hillshade. Next steps an agent can do here: roof-plane fitting with RANSAC (open3d), generating extruded meshes with stepped and cantilevered tiers (University Hall widens at floors 9 and 17), and exporting glTF. Points off: classification in this dataset is unreliable; data for post-2017 buildings must come from Overture; and facade detail (windows, concrete panel rhythm) needs human-reviewed modelling. AI agents struggle with artistic judgement and cannot see their own renders well without screenshots.

v.owner_effort: 1) Unblock these hosts, if wanted: clearinghouse.isgs.illinois.edu + data.isgs.illinois.edu (2022 LiDAR); maps.uic.edu (+ fm.uic.edu) (official building list); polyhaven.com + dl.polyhaven.org + ambientcg.com (free CC0 materials); commons.wikimedia.org + upload.wikimedia.org (licensed photos); data.cityofchicago.org (current footprints, optional). 2) The single most valuable thing: a photo survey of the ~15–25 'hero' buildings on an OVERCAST day, which avoids hard shadows baked into textures. For each facade, shoot straight-on photos from a few distances, close-ups of concrete and brick, ground-floor entrances, windows, signage and the plaza, plus a slow walking video of each route players will take. Phone camera is fine. Estimate 1–3 days. 3) Note what changed since 2017 (new buildings, demolished buildings, construction) so agents can patch the data. 4) Playtest and judge 'does this look like UIC?'. The owner's eye is the quality bar. 5) If realism outranks the browser, decide whether to buy or borrow a Windows gaming PC for an Unreal Engine 5 path; agents cannot run UE5 in this container.
risks: Expectation risk (biggest): 'close to GTA 6' at street level is not achievable by a solo owner plus AI agents on any platform. Accepting this early avoids disappointment and wasted months.
Data age: the 2017 LiDAR and the ~2015 footprint copy miss newer UIC construction and recent demolitions. Cross-check with Overture and the owner's photos.
LiDAR classification errors: on this Geiger-mode dataset most tall-building points are labelled vegetation. Use footprints to separate buildings from trees.

Coordinate pitfall: EPT is in Web Mercator (EPSG:3857), whose horizontal distances are about 1.34x too large at Chicago. Agents must reproject to a local metric frame or the campus will be the wrong size.

Legal: any texture or mesh derived from Google Street View, Earth or 3D Tiles violates the Google Maps Platform Terms (no content creation, no bulk download, no caching). CC BY-SA photos (Wikimedia, Mapillary) carry share-alike obligations that need an attribution/credits page.
ISGS 2022 data terms and current Chicago Data Portal terms are unverified; the City's disclaimer historically allowed it to demand you stop using its data.
Platform risk: the realism ceiling in the browser is well below UE5. Switching to UE5 breaks the 'AI agents build and test everything in a container' workflow and the existing three.js/Colyseus plan.
Scope creep: realistic facades for 50+ Brutalist buildings is a lot of modelling. Without a hero/background tier split it will not finish.
Several benchmark facts (GTA 6 budget, staff, dates, comparable projects) could not be re-verified because the web-search budget ran out mid-task. They are marked (unverified).
v.can_combine_with: This is the foundation layer for every rendering approach. (a) three.js browser build: LiDAR/footprint-derived meshes plus CC0 PBR materials plus baked lightmaps or HDRI lighting. (b) Unreal Engine 5 desktop build: the same meshes as blockout, hand-detailed hero buildings, Lumen and Nanite. (c) Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles: usable only inside Google's terms as a live-streamed backdrop for distant city or skyline, never as source for textures or models. Our own LiDAR geometry can replace it for collision and gameplay. (d) Owner-captured photogrammetry or Gaussian splats of a few hero spots (Quad, University Hall base, Halsted entrance), placed onto the accurate LiDAR massing. (e) Procedural facade generation (window grids, concrete panel rhythm) driven by per-building parameters (height, stories, tier setbacks) taken from this data.
v.verdict_for_this_project:
Use this data pipeline regardless of the renderer: it is free, legally clean (public domain + MIT) and already working here. It answers 'are the buildings the right size and shape?' with about 1–4 m accuracy (University Hall: LiDAR 104.3 m vs published 103 m). Do NOT expect data to deliver 'looks real up close'; that comes from lighting, materials and hand detail.

GTA 6 benchmark (all unverified this session, from widely reported coverage): built by Rockstar Games, whose credits run to thousands of people across many studios. Development lasted roughly a decade, on the proprietary RAGE engine. Analysts estimate the budget at $1–2B+ (never confirmed). Release was delayed to Nov 19, 2026, on PS5/Xbox Series only at launch. 'Vice City' is a stylized, compressed Miami built from extensive on-location reference and hand modelling, not a 1:1 scan. No small team matches that.

Ranked 'looks real' features for a small AI-built project (impact / effort):
1) Lighting and global illumination plus sky/sun/HDRI and good tone-mapping: highest impact; low effort in UE5 (Lumen), medium in browser (baked lightmaps plus HDRI).
2) Correct scale and massing: very high impact, low effort (this data).
3) PBR materials, specifically weathered concrete with stains and board/panel joints, and brick: very high impact, medium effort (CC0 libraries plus owner photos).
4) Atmospheric haze/fog and depth: high impact, low effort.
5) Vegetation (Chicago trees, lawns; LiDAR gives tree positions): high impact, medium effort; heavy for the browser.
6) Window detail and depth (recessed Netsch windows, reflections): high impact, medium–high effort.
7) Post-processing (bloom, SSAO, subtle color grade, motion blur): medium impact, low effort.
8) Small clutter (lamp posts, benches, signs, bike racks, trash cans, CTA signage, cracks, puddles): medium–high impact, high effort.
9) Reflections (SSR or ray tracing on glass and wet ground): medium impact, low in UE5 and hard in the browser.
10) People and cars: high 'alive' impact but high effort, and bad animation looks worse than none.

What is achievable for this team, street level / aerial (estimates, unverified):
- Browser (three.js/WebGPU), AI-built in this container: 3–4 / 6. Looks like a polished architectural-visualization site, clearly a game. Runs on any laptop; multiplayer easy.
- Desktop UE5, AI-assisted but owner needs a gaming PC and to do editor work: 5–6 (up to 7 in small hand-polished spots) / 7. About 2015–2018 AAA in places, uneven elsewhere. This is the best realism-per-effort; it gives up the 'agents build and test everything' workflow and the browser.
- Desktop Unity HDRP: 4–5 / 6. Similar to UE5 with more manual lighting work; no reason to prefer it here.
- Phones: 2–3 / 4.
- Browser plus Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles backdrop: 2–3 up close / 8 from the air, and legally restricted.
- GTA 6 for reference: 10 / 10.

Recommendation: keep the browser plan only if multiplayer reach matters more than the last 2–3 realism points. If 'buildings look real' is truly #1, run a one-week UE5 spike on one hero block (University Hall plus the Quad) using this data and the owner's photos before committing.

claim_checks.claim: Campus splat download is 'hundreds of MB'
claim_checks.correction_or_note: In my measurement, chunked .RAD LoD output was about 25 bytes per splat (5.2 MB for 200K splats, no spherical harmonics), and SOG was about 6 bytes per splat. v.score_challenges:
Street-level realism 6 is slightly inflated for this owner's stated goal (GTA 6 in play). The report itself says the moving experience is about 5 to 6, while the whole game is seen in motion under a third-person camera. Most of the world will be mesh filler, because only 4 to 6 hero sites are realistic to capture. The baked-light vs dynamic-light mismatch shows at every seam between splat and mesh and on every character. Adjusted: 5 as a hero-landmark add-on. Stills of hero spots can still hit 7 to 8, and the report is honest about this. Aerial 3 is fair.

AI-buildability 6 is slightly inflated. I tested in this container: format conversion, SOG and Spark .RAD LoD building do run on CPU. Collision voxels and meshes and floater filtering in splat-transform do NOT run without a GPU (error: 'writeVoxel requires a createDevice function for GPU voxelization'). Agents also cannot train splats, cannot judge visual quality, and cannot receive multi-GB phone captures easily (no transfer path is defined). Spark's desktop budget of 2.5M is fixed by platform, not GPU, so agents must also build adaptive quality for iGPU laptops without being able to test on one. Adjusted: 5.

Also note that all realism scores should be read against a budget reality the report never states. No browser approach, and no small-team approach, approaches GTA 6, which is a multi-year AAA production. A native engine (Unreal Engine 5 with Lumen/Nanite and photogrammetry-derived, de-lit PBR materials) is the only realistic route to 'GTA-like' dynamic lighting. It would cost the browser + multiplayer-in-a-link plan, and it would be harder for GPU-less agents to build and test.
missed_issues: splat-transform collision/voxel output and --filter-floaters require a GPU (WebGPU). I tested this in the container: both fail with --gpu cpu. Splat-derived collision meshes and automated floater cleanup cannot be produced by agents here, so footprint-extruded collision is the only agent-side path (unless a software-Vulkan fallback works; untested).

Renderer lock-in conflict. Spark is WebGL2 (WebGLRenderer). three.js's own splat addon is WebGPU-only and has no streaming LoD. If the mesh world later moves to WebGPURenderer for better lighting and post-processing (which a 'GTA-like' goal pushes toward), Spark compatibility is undocumented. Pick the renderer before investing.
Spark's 2.5M desktop default is chosen by platform, not GPU. iGPU laptops are not protected automatically, so the game needs a quality setting or an adaptive lodSplatScale.

No data-transfer path from the owner's phone to the agents' container. Raw videos and frames for one building are GBs. GitHub's 100 MB per-file limit and LFS quotas, plus blocked hosts, mean a storage route (e.g., a cloud bucket) has to be chosen and possibly unblocked.

Full-campus splat size is likely 1 to 2.5 GB (measured about 25 bytes/splat for chunked .RAD). That exceeds GitHub Pages' 1 GB site limit, so a real object store or CDN (e.g., R2 or S3) is needed. 'Hundreds of MB' only holds for the hero-only scope.

The report's combination idea (c), filling roofs and the tower top from photorealistic 3D tiles (Google tiles via tile.googleapis.com, which is reachable), probably conflicts with Google Map Tiles API terms on caching, extraction and derivative use. That needs the other researcher's ToS check before anyone plans on it (unverified).

Better route for the realism goal that the report undersells: use the same captures for photogrammetry to build de-lit PBR textures and materials on modeled buildings. This keeps the real stains and weathering of the Netsch concrete while supporting dynamic sun, shadows, day/night and wet surfaces, which is what actually makes GTA look real. Splats bake light in, and that is the opposite of the GTA look.

Platform honesty is missing. If realism truly outranks browser and multiplayer, a native UE5 build (Lumen, Nanite, photogrammetry assets) has a far higher ceiling. It costs the instant-link multiplayer and makes agent development and testing harder without a GPU. Neither browser nor UE5 indie reaches GTA 6, which is a multi-year AAA production.

Ground-truth scale and georeferencing. Phone splats have arbitrary scale and orientation, so each needs alignment to Overture footprints. This is fiddly, and agents cannot visually verify it without a GPU render.

The Spark demo evidence (third-person controller, STARSPEED) uses AI-generated worlds, and I found no such example in the Spark repo itself. There is no public precedent of a captured real-campus walkable multiplayer splat game. The UCSB capstone is a viewer, not a game.
The source for the AMD/World Labs acquisition is a small local paper. Confirm via AMD or World Labs before treating it as fact.

Every vendor price and ToS (Scaniverse, Polycam, KIRI, Postshot, RealityScan, Luma) and the UIC policy pages could not be independently re-verified: they were proxy-blocked and the search budget was exhausted. The owner should read the Scaniverse ToS and the UIC SMC policy directly before capturing or publishing. Hosts to unblock for verification: nianticspatial.com, today.uic.edu, police.uic.edu, poly.cam, realityscan.com, sparkjs.dev, worldlabs.ai.

claim_checks.correction_or_note: In uhall.npy, points more than 30 m above ground: class 5 = 39,313 and class 6 = 6,542, so 86% are labelled vegetation. Points more than 95 m above ground: class 5 = 8,731 and class 6 = 6,542. Splitting buildings from trees by footprint, not by LiDAR class, is the correct mitigation.

claim_checks.claim: LiDAR-derived University Hall height of 104.3 m matches the published 103 m, which shows the pipeline is accurate to about 1–4 m
claim_checks.correction_or_note: The CSV gives h98 = 104.3 m and h50 = 103.3 m. That agrees with the ~338 ft / 103 m already cited in the repo's campus-research.md (Wikipedia/UIC Library). But only two buildings (University Hall, SEO) were checked against independent figures. The 98th percentile includes rooftop equipment. Ground is a local median of class-2 points. 'About 1–4 m accuracy' across all 858 buildings is extrapolated, not measured. The skyscrapercenter URL could not be fetched (blocked).

claim_checks.claim: EPT data is in Web Mercator, which inflates horizontal distances about 1.34x at Chicago
claim_checks.correction_or_note: ept.json srs = EPSG:3857, and 1/cos(41.87°) = 1.343. This is correct and important for agents.

claim_checks.claim: City of Chicago building footprints on GitHub are MIT-licensed, about 2015, 820,606 footprints, with 252 of 869 bbox footprints having STORIES
claim_checks.correction_or_note: LICENSE.txt is MIT ('Copyright (c) 2013 City of Chicago'). I re-counted: 820,606 records, 869 in the bbox, 252 with STORIES > 0. The files are dated Aug 2015, but within the bbox the latest EDIT_DATE is 2010, so the UIC content is effectively a 2010 snapshot. All 869 are flagged ACTIVE and none carry DEMOLISHED data, so there is no demolition information. One correction: MIT 'Software' wording applied to data is unusual but permissive.

claim_checks.correction_or_note: Overture's own attribution doc gives the Buildings theme license as ODbL, with OSM, Microsoft ML footprints (ODbL), Esri Community Maps (CC BY 4.0) and others as sources. Any Overture-patched building layer that is shipped carries ODbL attribution and share-alike duties on the derived database. The repo's tech-architecture.md says 'mixed ODbL / CDLA-Permissive', which also appears outdated against the current docs.

claim_checks.claim: 17 U.S.C. §120(a) makes photos and a 3D game recreation of UIC buildings generally fine
claim_checks.correction_or_note: §120(a) covers 'pictures, paintings, photographs, or other pictorial representations'. Whether an interactive 3D model counts as a 'pictorial representation' is not clearly settled. Also, Architectural Works copyright protection applies only to buildings built after Dec 1, 1990. That makes the 1960s Netsch buildings even lower-risk, while newer buildings such as the ARC rely on §120. Not re-fetched (Cornell LII blocked); this is not legal advice.

v.score_challenges:
Street-level 4 is slightly inflated for what this approach actually delivers. On its own, the LiDAR plus footprint data gives extruded or roof-fitted boxes, which is about 2/10 at street level. The 4 is borrowed from rendering work (CC0 materials, lighting) that is not part of this approach and has not been demonstrated. I adjust it to 3. Aerial 6 is fair.

The UE5 street-level estimate of 5–6 (up to 7) is also optimistic for this team. It assumes 'hand-modelled hero buildings' and 'editor work'. The team is a non-coder with no 3D-art experience plus AI agents that cannot run the UE5 editor here. Without a hired 3D artist or bought asset packs, 4–5 is more honest.

AI buildability 8 is mostly earned. I confirmed the fetch, density, classification and height outputs exist and are reproducible from the scratchpad. But the hard parts are still unproven: RANSAC roof fitting, stepped and cantilevered meshes, glTF export, and patching post-2017 buildings. Facade realism needs artistic judgement that agents handle poorly. I adjust it to 7. One point the researcher missed in its favour: Blender can run headless on CPU in this container, so agents can script facade geometry and render CPU screenshots to check their own work.
missed_issues: Overture Buildings are ODbL (per current Overture attribution docs), not 'legally clean'. Patching post-2017 buildings from Overture brings ODbL attribution and share-alike on the shipped building database. Plan a data/LICENSE and credits entry, or model the new buildings from the owner's photos instead.

The GitHub footprint copy is older than claimed for UIC: the latest EDIT_DATE in the bbox is 2010 (not 2015), and every record is ACTIVE with no demolition info. Buildings built or demolished after about 2010 are wrong in the footprints, and those after spring 2017 are also missing from the LiDAR. The researcher's own recollection is that this includes some of East Campus's newest landmarks, such as the Academic and Residential Complex (about 2019) and the Computer Design Research and Learning Center (about 2022) (unverified). The owner should list these during the photo survey.
Height accuracy was validated against only 2 buildings. Before agents rely on the CSV, run a broader check against more published heights or the STORIES field (252 available).

The team has no 3D artist. Both the browser and UE5 paths depend on 'hand-modelled hero buildings', which nobody on the team can do. The realistic options are (a) a paid freelance 3D artist or bought asset packs (cost not estimated in the report), (b) procedural facades scripted by agents, or (c) owner-captured photogrammetry or Gaussian splats. The report under-budgets this.

Blender (headless, CPU Cycles/EEVEE-less rendering, Python API) is a missed middle path. Agents can generate and texture facade meshes and render verification screenshots in this GPU-less container, then export glTF to three.js, or FBX/USD to UE5 later.

Freedom-of-panorama nuance: it is unsettled whether §120 covers 3D interactive models. Pre-Dec-1990 buildings (most Netsch work) have no Architectural Works protection at all, which lowers risk. UIC trademarks remain separate.
Google Earth (the consumer app) is under the Google Earth Additional Terms, not the GMP Terms. The researcher conflated them, though both are restrictive.
Browser player-hardware claims are unsourced. Realistic lighting plus vegetation from the LiDAR tree positions will need quality tiers for integrated-GPU laptops.

Several cited sources (skyscrapercenter, USGS Geiger-mode page, Mapillary help, UE license, Cornell LII) were not reachable from this container in my session. Their claims rest on the researcher's prior fetches or general knowledge.

The shared web-search budget (200 per turn) was exhausted before this check, so the GTA 6, UE5 licence, Mapillary, ISGS and Chicago Data Portal claims are unverified. The owner can ask for a follow-up search turn.
